questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the key difference between Salesforce record ownership (OwnerId, OWD, role hierarchy) and data ownership in the governance sense?
options: There is no real difference; they describe the same thing

Record ownership is a security/access mechanism controlling visibility of individual records; data ownership is business-level accountability for a data type's accuracy and standards across the whole org
Record ownership only applies to custom objects, while data ownership only applies to standard objects
Data ownership is set automatically whenever a record is created
questions.explain: Record ownership controls who can see/edit a specific record; data ownership is the accountability for the data type as a whole -- a sales rep can own many records without being the governance-level data owner for that object.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue a sales rep who owns a hundred Account records is unlikely to also be the Account object's governance-level data owner?
options: Sales reps are never allowed to own Salesforce records
Data ownership in the governance sense requires authority over org-wide definitions and standards, which is a different scope than day-to-day record handling
Only Salesforce admins can be record owners
The Account object cannot have a data owner at all
questions.explain: Data ownership is about setting standards and resolving disputes at the object level, which requires a different kind of authority than owning individual records day to day.

questions.q: In the Account-data example (touched by Sales, Marketing, Finance, and Support), what problem does this lesson say results from no one being accountable for the object as a whole?
options: Salesforce automatically locks the object until an owner is assigned
Each function optimizes for its own use and the data drifts -- e.g. Sales leaves a field blank because it doesn't affect deals, hurting Marketing's segmentation and Finance's billing accuracy
The object becomes permanently read-only
Nothing changes, since each department already governs its own fields independently
questions.explain: Without a named owner with authority to settle standards, each department optimizes locally and the shared data degrades for everyone else's use case.

questions.q: When two departments (e.g. Sales and Marketing) both believe they own the same object (Contact), what resolution approach does this lesson recommend?
options: Always default ownership to whichever department created the object first
Delete the object and recreate two separate ones
Split accountability by attribute -- e.g. Sales owns sales-readiness fields, Marketing owns consent/subscription fields -- with contested splits escalated to a shared governance body
Assign ownership randomly to avoid political conflict
questions.explain: The lesson recommends splitting accountability by attribute rather than picking one department as the sole winner, with disputes about the split itself escalated to governance.

questions.q: What does this lesson say makes a data-ownership assignment durable enough to survive staff turnover?
options: Keeping the assignment informal and known only to the current data owner
A maintained ownership register naming the data owner and steward per major object, with a recurring review date, owned by a body like the governance committee
Re-deciding ownership from scratch every time someone leaves the company
Assigning ownership permanently to the Salesforce platform itself rather than to a person or role
questions.explain: A documented, periodically-reviewed register (not a fact living only in one person's head) is what keeps the ownership assignment usable after the original decision-maker moves on.
